lesson.title: A Nation Explains Itself: The Declaration of Independence
lesson.summary: Adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, the Declaration of Independence announced the colonies' break from Britain and grounded that decision in a bold statement of natural rights.
lesson.body:
By the spring of 1776, more than a year of fighting since Lexington and Concord, the rejection of the Olive Branch Petition, and the wide popularity of Thomas Paine's Common Sense had pushed the Second Continental Congress toward a step that had seemed unthinkable just two years earlier: a formal break from Great Britain. On June 7, 1776, Richard Henry Lee of Virginia introduced a resolution declaring that the colonies were, and of right ought to be, free and independent states.

While debate over Lee's resolution continued, Congress appointed a committee of five delegates to draft a formal declaration explaining the decision to the world. The committee included John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston, but the actual writing fell mainly to Thomas Jefferson of Virginia, whose skill with the pen was already well regarded among his colleagues in Congress. Working largely alone over about two weeks in rented rooms in Philadelphia, Jefferson produced a draft that the committee reviewed and lightly revised before submitting it to the full Congress for debate.

Congress formally voted for independence on July 2, 1776, when it approved Lee's resolution. John Adams believed at the time that this date, not the fourth, would be remembered as the nation's birthday. Instead, it was July 4, 1776, the day Congress finished editing and formally adopted the text of the Declaration itself, that became the date fixed in American memory. Congress had trimmed and altered Jefferson's draft in a number of places, most notably removing a passage condemning the slave trade, a change that reflected the objections of delegates from slaveholding colonies and left slavery's contradiction with the Declaration's own language unresolved for generations to come.

The document's most enduring passage was not its long list of grievances against King George III, though that list filled most of its length, but its opening statement of principle: that all men are created equal and are endowed with unalienable rights, including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. These ideas drew heavily on Enlightenment political philosophy, particularly the writings of John Locke on natural rights and the legitimate basis of government.

Most delegates signed the engrossed parchment copy beginning August 2, 1776, with John Hancock, the president of Congress, adding his famously large and bold signature first. Copies of the printed Declaration were also sent to Continental Army units and read aloud to soldiers and civilians across the colonies. The Declaration did not win the war by itself, but it transformed the conflict's meaning, turning a rebellion over taxes and parliamentary authority into a founding argument for a new kind of nation built on the consent and equality of its citizens, at least in principle.
